title: CapEx vs OpEx Classification and Commit-to-Forecast Harmonization
author: Samantha Ortiz
body:
Summary:
This playbook clarifies how Redwood classifies expenditures as CapEx versus OpEx, how committed procurement contracts feed into budget and forecast models, and prescribes an operational handoff between procurement, legal, and finance to ensure consistent GL coding and revenue recognition triggers. It is intended for finance managers, procurement leads, legal reviewers, and product leaders making purchasing decisions that span multiple financial periods.

Scope and objective:
- Scope: Applies to all third-party contracts, vendor purchase orders, cloud/infra commitments, equipment purchases, annual software licenses, and dedicated capacity commitments (Redwood Dedicated). Excludes routine operational consumables under $5k unless part of a multi-year commitment.
- Objective: Reduce forecast variance from procurement commitments by standardizing classification, timing, and communication steps so forecasts and SOWs accurately reflect economic substance.

Key definitions:
- CapEx (Capital Expenditure): Outlays that result in the acquisition or enhancement of a long-lived asset where benefits extend beyond 12 months. Examples: on-prem GPU racks, on-prem software perpetual licenses with significant implementation costs, hardware purchases.
- OpEx (Operating Expenditure): Short-lived costs consumed within the operating cycle or within 12 months. Examples: monthly cloud usage, short-term contractor engagements, routine SaaS subscriptions under 12 months.
- Commit: Any signed contract, PO, or legally binding order that creates an obligation for future cash flow.
- Forecast window: The next 12 months (rolling) plus a high-level 24–36 month view for capacity planning.

Classification rules (decision tree):
1) Is there a tangible or intangible asset created with useful life > 12 months? If yes -> CapEx.
2) Is the agreement payable over multiple years but the vendor delivers a service only (no transferable asset)? If yes -> OpEx (unless contract contains a purchase option that transfers control).
3) Is there a significant implementation or customization cost that qualifies for capitalization under accounting policy? If yes -> portion may be CapEx.
4) If total contract value exceeds $250k and term >= 24 months, escalate to finance-legal for review regardless of initial classification.

Financial impacts and forecasting behavior:
- CapEx purchases should be budgeted against the CapEx budget line and included in the capital request form. CapEx will be amortized over the defined useful life; forecast models should consume amortization expense into the monthly P&L and reflect cash outflow timing separately in the cash forecast.
- OpEx commitments appear directly in the monthly operating forecast (P&L) as expense when incurred and in the cash forecast by payment schedule. For usage-based contracts, use 3-month rolling actuals to project near-term spend.
- Multi-year committed spend with fixed payments should be surfaced in both the one-year operating forecast (for the portion falling in year 1) and in the long-range commitment schedule (for years 2+).

Commit-to-Forecast operational handoff (procurement -> finance):
1) Procurement obtains signed contract/PO and uploads a copy to the contract repository with standardized metadata fields populated: vendor, contract_id, start_date, end_date, total_value, payment_schedule, renewal_terms, contract_owner, cost_center, product_code, and GL_suggested_code.
2) Procurement tags the contract with preliminary classification: CAPEX or OPEX and a short rationale.
3) Procurement notifies Finance via the procurement-finance slack channel and opens a Finance Intake ticket including the contract_id and the GL_suggested_code.
4) Finance reviews within 5 business days and either:
   - Confirms classification and assigns final GL code, or
   - Requests additional economic substance analysis (e.g., SOW details or asset schedules).
5) Upon confirmation, finance updates the forecasting model and the centralized commitment register.

Approval matrix (simplified):
- <$25k: Procurement lead approval.
- $25k–$250k: Procurement + Product manager approval.
- $250k–$1M: Procurement + Product + Finance director sign-off.
- >$1M or multi-year > 24 months: Procurement + Finance + Legal + CFO approval.
Note: exceptions for security or compliance-sensitive vendors require Legal review regardless of dollar amount.

Template: contract metadata (as text table)
| Field | Description | Example |
| vendor | Legal vendor name | VectorCloud Inc. |
| contract_id | Internal identifier | VC-2025-013 |
| start_date | Effective date | 2025-04-01 |
| end_date | Expiration date | 2028-03-31 |
| total_value | Sum of all obligations | $1,200,000 |
| payment_schedule | Calendar of payments | Quarterly in arrears |
| classification_prelim | Procurement suggested (CAPEX/OPEX) | CAPEX (hardware) |
| cost_center | Owning cost center | Infra-Platform |
| GL_suggested_code | Suggested GL mapping | 5600-Servers-Capex |

Journal entry examples (for accounting team) - included as illustrative only:
- CapEx purchase (cash purchase of servers $600,000):
  Dr: IT Equipment (Fixed Assets) $600,000
  Cr: Cash/Bank $600,000
  Subsequent monthly amortization (5 year straight-line):
  Dr: Amortization Expense $10,000
  Cr: Accumulated Amortization $10,000

- Multi-year SaaS commitment with upfront prepayment (OpEx over time):
  On payment of annual invoice $360,000:
  Dr: Prepaid Expense $360,000
  Cr: Cash $360,000
  Monthly amortization to expense (12 months):
  Dr: SaaS Expense $30,000
  Cr: Prepaid Expense $30,000

Revenue recognition and billing interaction notes (where procurement affects revrec):
- Dedicated capacity customer contracts that create vendor-like obligations (e.g., Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity) should be aligned with committed vendor costs. If customer billing is usage-based but vendor contract is fixed, finance must ensure margin recognition rules are consistent and disclose any timing mismatch in internal margin reports.
- When procurement enters into vendor contracts that have customer-pass-through billing implications, add a cost-pass-through flag in metadata so Product and Finance can coordinate billing rules and tax treatment.

Operational checklists (procurement + finance + legal):
Procurement checklist before submit to Finance:
- [ ] Signed contract stored in repo with metadata completed
- [ ] Payment schedule verified (currency, taxes, fees)
- [ ] Preliminary classification and rationale documented
- [ ] Vendor W-9 / EIN or equivalent collected
- [ ] Vendor insurance and security attestation recorded if required

Finance checklist for intake review:
- [ ] Confirm classification or request analysis (within 5 business days)
- [ ] Assign GL codes and update budget vs actual trackers
- [ ] Update cash forecast and capital request logs
- [ ] Tag contract for revrec impact if it affects customer billing or margin reporting

Legal checklist for procurement handoff:
- [ ] Review termination and renewal clauses for automatic renewals
- [ ] Confirm indemnity, IP, data-residency, and escrow clauses as required
- [ ] Confirm approval matrix and signature authority executed
- [ ] Flag any regulatory or export-control restrictions

Exception and escalation workflow:
- If Finance cannot confirm classification in 5 business days, escalate to Finance Director with a one-page economic substance memo prepared by Procurement.
- If classification materially impacts reported results (> $250k P&L timing shift or > $500k cash misstatement), route to CFO for final decision.
- Legal escalates to General Counsel for any contract that includes unusual IP, escrow, KMS, or customer data residency obligations.

Forecasting mechanics and model inputs (practical guidance):
- For subscription contracts: load invoice schedule and map to monthly forecast lines. If annual upfront is used, show both cash and expense amortization rows.
- For committed cloud/infrastructure credits: translate committed units to expected monthly usage by applying a conservative 75% utilization factor for year 1 and 85% thereafter.
- For headcount or third-party services tied to product features: include ramp assumptions (start month, % productivity ramp per month, termination notice windows).

Sample GL mapping (examples):
- Hardware CapEx: 5600-Servers-Capex
- Dedicated capacity OpEx (cloud reserved): 6100-Cloud-Reserved-OpEx
- SaaS subscriptions: 6300-SaaS-Subscriptions
- Professional services / Implementation: 6500-Consulting (split between CapEx-qualifying portion)

Data and templates (where to find them):
- Contract repository: /systems/contracts (link internal)
- Commitment register (master): /finance/commitment-register (link internal)
- Budget submission form: /finance/forms/capex-request (link internal)
- Forecast model template: /finance/models/monthly-forecast-v2 (link internal)

Frequently asked questions (FAQ):
Q: A 3-year SaaS contract includes a perpetual license for a plug-in component. How to classify?
A: Separate the transaction: allocate the purchase price between the perpetual license (CapEx, if meets capitalization criteria) and the service subscription (OpEx). Documentation must include allocation methodology.

Q: What if a vendor charges an initial implementation fee and recurring support?
A: Capitalize the implementation fee if it meets capitalization guidelines; treat ongoing support as OpEx. Keep supporting documentation (invoices, SOW) in the contract repository.

Q: How do we handle FX or multi-currency commitments?
A: Use functional currency conversion at the contract effective date for budgeting. Finance must maintain FX variance lines in the forecast to capture realized differences at payment time.

Related governance notes:
- All classification disputes that meet the thresholds in the approval matrix must be documented with decision rationale and retained for audit (minimum 7 years).
- Procurement must ensure metadata completeness; missing metadata will extend Finance review windows.
